title: 7 Best Weed Killers in 2026: Pick the Chemistry for the Job
metaDescription: Roundup Super Concentrate is the best weed killer for clearing beds to the roots; Tenacity is #1 for lawns. 7 picks, plus rainfast, pet and timing advice.
keywords: what is the best weed killer for tough weeds
what is the best weed killer on the market
intro:
The best weed killer for most homeowners is Roundup Weed & Grass Killer Super Concentrate for clearing beds, fence lines and overgrown patches down to the roots, and Tenacity Turf Herbicide for weeds growing inside a lawn you want to keep. Those two cover the most common jobs, and five more picks below handle gravel, quick cleanups, budgets, prevention and non-synthetic spraying.

Picking by brand or by the scariest-sounding label is how most people end up disappointed. A product strong enough to clear a gravel lot will also kill the lawn next to it, and a lawn-safe spray barely slows down grass in patio cracks. This guide ranks seven weed killers by job, then answers the questions people actually search: what is strongest, what works on lawns, what survives rain, how long it takes and how to keep pets safe.
quickAnswer: Use Roundup Super Concentrate or budget Compare-N-Save glyphosate to kill beds and fence lines to the roots, and Tenacity for weeds inside a cool-season lawn. Save Ortho GroundClear Year Long for gravel with no tree roots nearby, and use Preen only after existing weeds are gone. Whatever you buy, the label sets the rate, the rainfast time and when pets can go back out.

sections.heading: Best Weed Killer: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Pick | Best for | Key spec |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roundup Super Concentrate | Clearing beds and fence lines to the roots | Non-selective, systemic concentrate |
| Tenacity Turf Herbicide | Weeds inside a cool-season lawn | Mesotrione, usable at seeding |
| Ortho GroundClear Year Long | Gravel and ground that should stay bare | Residual, up to a year per Ortho |
| Spectracide Weed & Grass Concentrate | Fast cleanup before an event | Contact action, wilting in hours |
| Compare-N-Save Concentrate | Acreage and long fence rows on a budget | 41% glyphosate |
| Preen Garden Weed Preventer | Keeping clean beds clean | Trifluralin pre-emergent granules |
| Green Gobbler 20% Vinegar | Cracks and edges without synthetics | 20% acetic acid |

There is no single strongest weed killer that suits every yard. The right product depends on three things: whether the weeds sit in grass you want to keep, whether you need the roots dead or only the tops, and whether you want the ground to stay bare afterward.

If the weeds are in your lawn, buy a selective product like Tenacity. If you are clearing a bed or fence line, use a systemic concentrate. Save residual vegetation killers for gravel with no tree roots nearby, and use a pre-emergent only after the existing weeds are gone.

sections.heading: The 7 Best Weed Killers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
These rankings come from each product's EPA-registered label: the active ingredient and its concentration, the weeds and sites it is labeled for, rainfast and re-entry directions, and how far one container goes. Owner feedback and cost per treated area broke ties. None of these products went through field trials for this guide, and nothing below is credited with results its label does not support.

### Best Overall: Roundup Weed & Grass Killer Super Concentrate
Roundup Super Concentrate is the jug to grab when a fence line, a neglected bed or the strip along a foundation needs to go back to bare soil, roots and all. It is non-selective and systemic: you dilute it in a pump sprayer, wet the leaves, and the chemistry travels down to the roots over the following days. The label lists one mix rate for ordinary weeds and a stronger one for tough perennials, and a single bottle makes a lot of spray, so the cost per treated square foot stays low. One caution matters more than any other. Bayer began moving its US residential lawn and garden line away from glyphosate in 2023, so the active ingredient depends on which version is on the shelf. Read the ingredient panel and use that label's rates, not the ones you remember from an older bottle. Expect yellowing within days and a full kill in one to two weeks, and keep it far away from any grass you want to keep.

**Pros:** Root kill on most weeds and grasses it lists; concentrate makes many gallons; clear mixing table; dries rainfast quickly.
**Cons:** Kills lawn grass as readily as weeds; the active ingredient varies by bottle; slow compared with contact sprays.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Roundup+Weed+Grass+Killer+Super+Concentrate&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Lawns: Tenacity Turf Herbicide
Tenacity solves the problem most homeowners actually have: weeds growing inside a lawn they want to keep. Its active ingredient, mesotrione, is tolerated by most cool-season grasses while broadleaf weeds, crabgrass and nimblewill are not. The feature that sets it apart is that the label permits use at seeding on many cool-season grasses, so you can clean up weeds and overseed in the same season instead of waiting weeks between the two. The bottle is small and costs more than a big-box jug, yet the label rate is measured in teaspoons per thousand square feet, so it covers a large lawn. For post-emergent spraying, the label calls for adding a nonionic surfactant. Treated weeds turn bright white within a week or two before they die, which is normal. Check the turf list before you buy: bermudagrass and some bentgrasses are injured, and warm-season results vary. Stubborn perennials usually need a second application.

**Pros:** Spares labeled turf while killing broadleaf and some grassy weeds; usable at seeding; tiny label rate stretches far; some pre-emergent action.
**Cons:** Injures bermudagrass and some other turf types; needs an added surfactant; slower than most lawn sprays.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Tenacity+Turf+Herbicide&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Gravel and Driveways: Ortho GroundClear Year Long Vegetation Killer
GroundClear Year Long is a total vegetation killer with a soil-residual ingredient. It kills what is green today and, according to Ortho, leaves enough activity in the top layer of soil to keep new growth from establishing for up to a year. That makes it efficient on a gravel parking pad, along the base of a chain-link fence, in the joints of a back path, or anywhere you want nothing to grow for a full season. The ready-to-use jug needs no mixing. The same staying power is the danger. Residual chemistry moves with rain toward lower ground, and tree roots reach far past the drip line, often under driveways and walks. Spraying it over the root zone of a maple or beside a hedge can injure plants you never touched. Follow the label's site restrictions, keep it off slopes that drain toward lawns or beds, and keep it well away from wells, ponds and streams.

**Pros:** Kills current growth and prevents new weeds for months; no mixing; ideal for gravel, fence rows and back-lot paths.
**Cons:** Can damage tree and shrub roots under the treated area; no replanting there; runoff risk on slopes.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ortho+GroundClear+Year+Long+Vegetation+Killer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Fast-Acting: Spectracide Weed & Grass Killer Concentrate
Spectracide's concentrate is built for quick visible results. Its contact-type chemistry burns down green tissue fast, and owners commonly report young annual weeds wilting the same day they spray. That suits deadline jobs: patio joints before a backyard party, a curb line before you sealcoat, or a strip along the siding before painters arrive. The trade-off is depth. Contact action does little to roots, so perennials such as dandelion, bindweed and quackgrass often regrow from the crown within weeks. Spectracide also sells several weed and grass killers with near-identical names and different active ingredients, so flip the bottle and confirm whether you have a pure contact formula or one blended with a systemic ingredient. Mix strictly to the label rate, aim only at the weed, and keep spray off lawn edges and garden plants. For a weed patch that keeps coming back, follow up with a systemic product instead of respraying every two weeks.

**Pros:** Visible wilting within hours on many annuals; inexpensive per mixed gallon; sold almost everywhere; good before events or sealing.
**Cons:** Perennial roots often survive; similar names hide different formulas; non-selective, so overspray browns grass.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Spectracide+Weed+Grass+Killer+Concentrate&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget Concentrate: Compare-N-Save Concentrate Grass & Weed Killer
Compare-N-Save is straight 41% glyphosate in a big jug, the same concentration farm stores have stocked for decades, at a small fraction of the price of name-brand consumer bottles. Rural owners use it for fence rows, the ground around sheds and outbuildings, dry ditches that do not carry water, and clearing a plot before a garden or new lawn goes in. Because glyphosate has little meaningful soil activity at label rates, you can usually replant once the waiting period printed on the label has passed, which is a big advantage over residual vegetation killers. The label lists separate rates for annual weeds, perennials and woody brush and requires gloves and eye protection when you handle the concentrate. The large container is the drawback on a small lot, and mixed spray loses strength after a day or so, so dilute only what you will use. Spray actively growing weeds on a calm, dry day for the best root kill.

**Pros:** Lowest cost per gallon of mixed spray; big jug suits acreage and long fence lines; root kill on labeled perennials; no added residual.
**Cons:** Results vary on waxy weeds without extra surfactant; more product than a small yard needs; concentrate demands real care when mixing.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Compare-N-Save+Concentrate+Grass+Weed+Killer+41%25+glyphosate&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Pre-Emergent: Preen Garden Weed Preventer
Preen is a granular pre-emergent built on trifluralin, which stops germinating seeds from forming roots. It does nothing to weeds you can already see, so the order matters: pull or kill the current weeds, shake Preen over the bed at the label rate, then water it in so it activates in the top layer of soil. Used that way around established perennials, shrubs and many transplanted vegetables, it cuts down the flush of seedlings that turns a freshly weeded bed into a chore again by July. The label sets reapplication intervals through the season and lists the plants it can be used around, so read it before you scatter granules near seeded rows. The big limitation is that it cannot tell weed seeds from flower or vegetable seeds; anything you sow directly in a treated bed will struggle. Sweep stray granules off walks and drives, and store the container where pets cannot reach it.

**Pros:** Stops many weed seeds from establishing; easy shaker application around plants; long list of labeled ornamentals and vegetables.
**Cons:** No effect on existing weeds; blocks seeds you sow too; needs repeat applications through the season.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Preen+Garden+Weed+Preventer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Non-Synthetic Option: Green Gobbler 20% Horticultural Vinegar
Green Gobbler is 20% acetic acid, four times the strength of kitchen vinegar, and it is far more hazardous to handle than its natural image suggests. At this strength the label warns of serious eye damage and skin irritation, so wear goggles and chemical-resistant gloves and keep children and pets clear while you spray. Applied full strength on a sunny, warm day, it dries out the leaves of young annual weeds within hours, which makes it useful in sidewalk cracks, gravel edges and paver joints when you want a fast result without a synthetic herbicide. It breaks down quickly in soil and leaves no lasting residue. The limits are real: it only affects the tissue it touches, so established perennials usually regrow from their roots, and repeat spraying adds up in cost. It is non-selective, so drift browns grass and garden plants. Spray on calm days, keep it off metal and stone you care about, and rinse the sprayer afterward.

**Pros:** Fast burn-down of young annuals in warm sun; no synthetic active ingredient; no lasting soil residue; handy for cracks and edges.
**Cons:** Can cause serious eye injury and skin burns; rarely kills perennial roots; costs more per square foot over repeat sprays.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Green+Gobbler+20%25+Horticultural+Vinegar&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: How Do You Choose a Weed Killer That Works?
sections.body:
Most disappointment with weed killer comes from buying the strongest-sounding bottle instead of the right chemistry. Three label questions sort every product on the shelf.

### Selective or non-selective?
A selective herbicide is designed to spare certain plants, usually lawn grass, while killing broadleaf weeds or specific grassy weeds. A non-selective product kills nearly any green plant it wets. Spot-spraying dandelions in a lawn with a non-selective jug is the classic expensive mistake, because every dead circle takes a season to fill back in.

### Systemic or contact?
Systemic products are absorbed through the leaves and carried down to the roots. They are slow, often one to two weeks, but they finish perennials. Contact products burn whatever they touch within hours and leave perennial roots alive to regrow.

### Post-emergent or pre-emergent?
Post-emergents kill weeds that are already up. Pre-emergents, such as Preen, create a barrier in the soil that stops seeds from rooting and do nothing to existing weeds. Residual vegetation killers do both, which is why they are the most likely to harm trees by accident.

### Match the product to the problem
| Problem | Product type | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dandelions and clover in a cool-season lawn | Selective post-emergent | Tenacity |
| Clearing a bed or fence line to the roots | Non-selective systemic | Roundup, Compare-N-Save |
| Quick cleanup of cracks | Non-selective contact | Spectracide, 20% vinegar |
| Gravel that should stay bare all year | Soil-residual killer | Ortho GroundClear Year Long |
| Seedlings in mulched beds | Granular pre-emergent | Preen |

Think about the place as well as the weed. A driveway edge that drains into the lawn, a bed under a mature tree and a fence line beside the vegetable garden each call for a different product even when the weeds look the same. If the growth is knee-high, knock it down first with one of the [best weed eaters](/best-weed-eater/) so your spray lands on fresh regrowth rather than old stems.

sections.heading: What Is the Strongest Weed Killer for Tough Weeds?
sections.body:
People searching for the strongest weed killer usually mean the one that keeps weeds from coming back. For established perennials, strength means reaching the roots, not burning the leaves fastest.

### Tough perennials: systemic is the answer
Bindweed, poison ivy, quackgrass, thistle and similar deep-rooted weeds need a systemic product applied to actively growing leaves. A glyphosate concentrate such as Compare-N-Save, mixed at the label's perennial rate, is the usual choice. Expect to spray twice: once to knock the plant down and again on any regrowth a few weeks later.

### Woody brush and vines
Most glyphosate labels list a higher rate for woody brush and vines. Cutting the stems and treating the fresh stumps, where the label allows it, often works better than spraying a tall thicket.

### Why extra strength backfires
Mixing double strength feels like insurance, but it is a label violation, and on some systemic products it scorches the leaves so quickly that the chemistry never travels to the roots. The weed looks dead for a week and then regrows. Use the rate listed for your specific weed.

### Strongest for bare ground
If you want the ground bare for a year, a residual product like Ortho GroundClear Year Long is the strongest tool available to homeowners. Use it only where no tree or shrub roots run underneath.

sections.heading: What Is the Best Weed Killer for Lawns?
sections.body:
For weeds mixed into turf, a selective lawn herbicide is the only sensible choice. Spraying anything non-selective on grass you want to keep trades a weed problem for a bare-patch problem.

### Cool-season lawns
On Kentucky bluegrass, tall fescue and perennial ryegrass, Tenacity is the standout because the label allows use at seeding on many of those grasses. A three-way broadleaf herbicide labeled for your grass is a cheaper option for dandelions, clover and plantain.

### Warm-season lawns
Bermudagrass, St. Augustine, zoysia and centipede each react differently to lawn herbicides, and some products that are safe on fescue injure them. Read the grass list on the label before buying anything, and skip products that do not name your species.

### Timing for the best result
Selective lawn sprays work best on weeds that are actively growing in mild weather. Many labels warn against spraying turf during high heat or drought dormancy. For perennial broadleaf weeds such as dandelion and ground ivy, early fall is often the most effective window, because the plants are moving sugars down to their roots and carry the herbicide with them.

### Mowing around a treatment
Leave a couple of days between mowing and spraying on both sides. Mowing first removes the leaf surface the spray needs; mowing too soon afterward cuts off treated leaves before the product has moved into the plant. A thick lawn cut high with a [self-propelled mower](/best-self-propelled-lawn-mower/) is also the cheapest long-term weed control there is.

sections.heading: Will Rain Wash Away Weed Killer? Choosing a Rainproof Option
sections.body:
Rain can wash weed killer off leaves before it works, and it can carry spray off pavement into storm drains. The fix is timing and reading the rainfast line on the label.

### What rainfast means
Labels list a rainfast period: the time the spray must dry on the leaves before rain no longer reduces its effect. It ranges from under an hour to several hours depending on the product. Once a product is rainfast, rain will not undo the treatment, though a few labels also warn against applying if heavy rain is forecast within a day or two.

### The best rain-proof habits
Spray on a dry morning with no rain expected for the rest of the day. Do not spray frozen or soggy ground, and do not spray on a slope that drains toward a lawn, a garden or water. Granular pre-emergents are different: many need watering in, so a light rain after application can actually help them.

### Keep it off pavement
Driveways and patios are where runoff starts. Spray only the weed in the crack, not the concrete around it, because product sitting on a hard surface washes straight to the curb with the next storm. If you are cleaning a driveway before sealing, kill the crack weeds, let them brown, and pull them before you reach for the [best driveway cleaner](/best-driveway-cleaner/) or sealer.

### Near water
Most home herbicides are not labeled for use near ponds, streams, wells or ditches that carry water. Unless the label specifically allows shoreline use, keep application well away.

sections.heading: Is Glyphosate Safe, and What Are the Alternatives?
sections.body:
Glyphosate is the most widely used herbicide in the world and remains the active ingredient in many home concentrates. It blocks an enzyme pathway plants need to build certain amino acids, a pathway animals do not have.

### Where the debate stands
The International Agency for Research on Cancer classified glyphosate as probably carcinogenic to humans in 2015. The US EPA has concluded that it is not likely to be carcinogenic when used according to the label, but a federal appeals court in 2022 found the agency's human health analysis inadequate, and the EPA withdrew that part of its interim decision while it continues the review. Bayer also moved its US consumer lawn and garden products away from glyphosate starting in 2023.

### Practical precautions
Use glyphosate only where you need a root kill, mix to the label rate, wear the gloves and eye protection the label lists, skip windy days, and wash exposed skin afterward. Keep people and pets off the area until it dries.

### Alternatives that work
Horticultural vinegar burns down young annuals but rarely kills perennial roots. Mulch two to three inches deep over clean soil blocks most annual weeds in beds. Boiling water poured on the crown kills young weeds in pavement cracks. Smothering overgrown ground with overlapping cardboard and mulch, or clear plastic through high summer, clears it in a couple of months with no waiting period before planting. Avoid salt remedies: salt sterilizes soil for years and damages concrete.

sections.heading: How Do You Apply Weed Killer Safely Around Pets and Kids?
sections.body:
Nearly every liquid herbicide label says to keep people and pets out of the treated area until the spray has dried. Treat that as the minimum.

### Before you spray
Pick a dry, calm morning when the yard can stay empty for several hours. Keep pets inside, and move toys, bowls and furniture out of the area. Wear the protective gear the label lists, which for concentrates usually means gloves and eye protection.

### Mixing a concentrate correctly
Mix outdoors where a spill cannot reach a drain. Fill the sprayer partway with water, add the measured concentrate, then top off and agitate. Use a dedicated measuring cup that never returns to the kitchen, and mix only what you will use that day. Keep one sprayer for non-selective products and label it, because residue can injure plants the next time you use it for fertilizer.

### Spraying technique
Use a coarse spray close to the weed, not a fine mist. Wet the leaves until they glisten but do not drip. Shield nearby plants with a piece of cardboard when you work close to them.

### After the job
Triple rinse empty containers and add the rinse water to the sprayer. Store leftovers in the original container on a high shelf or locked cabinet; most pet poisonings involving lawn products come from chewed containers and spilled concentrate, not dried lawns. If a child or pet swallows a product, read the first aid section and call for help with the container in hand. The US Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222. After weeding, a quick pass with a [cordless leaf blower](/best-cordless-leaf-blower/) clears clippings and seed off hard surfaces.

sections.heading: How Long Does Weed Killer Take to Work?
sections.body:
How quickly a weed killer works depends on its chemistry, the weather and the size of the weed.

### Typical timelines
| Product type | First visible change | Full result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contact spray or 20% vinegar | Hours on young weeds in sun | One to three days |
| Systemic glyphosate | Yellowing in several days | One to two weeks |
| Selective lawn herbicide | Curling or bleaching in a week | Two to three weeks, sometimes a second spray |
| Pre-emergent | No visible change | Prevents seedlings for the labeled interval |

### What speeds it up
Warm, mild weather with good soil moisture and young, actively growing weeds give the fastest kill. Drought-stressed weeds in July absorb far less product, and cool weather slows systemic products down.

### Pre-emergent timing
Crabgrass begins germinating when shallow soil holds around 55 degrees Fahrenheit for several days, so pre-emergents go down in early spring. Too late and the seedlings are already up; too early in a warm region and the barrier can thin before germination peaks.

### Wait before pulling
Leave sprayed perennials in place until they have browned completely. Pulling or digging too soon leaves living roots behind, and they regrow.

mistakes.title: Spot-spraying the lawn with a non-selective product
mistakes.body: A total weed and grass killer cannot tell a dandelion from bluegrass. Spot-treating a lawn with one leaves a pattern of dead circles that take a full season to fill in. Use a selective lawn herbicide labeled for your grass type and keep the non-selective jug for beds, edges and gravel.

mistakes.title: Mixing stronger than the label rate
mistakes.body: Doubling the dose is a label violation and often backfires. Some systemic sprays scorch the leaves so fast at high concentration that the chemistry never reaches the roots, so the weed comes back. Extra product also means more runoff and more risk to nearby plants. Measure carefully and use the rate for your weed.

mistakes.title: Coating the whole driveway to catch a few cracks
mistakes.body: Concrete and asphalt do not absorb herbicide, so spray that lands on them sits on the surface and washes to the storm drain with the next rain. Aim the nozzle at the weed in the crack, use a coarse spray close to the target, and treat only what is green.

mistakes.title: Using a residual killer near trees
mistakes.body: Soil-active vegetation killers stay in the ground for months, and tree roots spread well beyond the canopy, often under driveways and walks. A residual product sprayed along a drive lined with maples can cause yellowing and dieback a season later. Use a non-residual product anywhere roots you value might reach.

mistakes.title: Spraying before rain or in wind
mistakes.body: Rain before the product is rainfast dilutes the dose and carries it off target, and even a light breeze can drift fine droplets onto a neighbor's hedge or your tomatoes. Check the forecast, spray on a calm, dry morning, and use a coarse nozzle setting held close to the weed.

faqs.q: What is the best weed killer on the market?
faqs.a: The best weed killer depends on the job. Roundup Super Concentrate is the best all-round choice for clearing beds and fence lines to the roots, Tenacity is best for weeds inside a cool-season lawn, and Ortho GroundClear Year Long is best for gravel that should stay bare. Read the label to confirm it lists your weeds, your site and, for lawns, your grass type.

faqs.q: What is the strongest weed killer?
faqs.a: For killing weeds to the roots, a 41% glyphosate concentrate such as Compare-N-Save, mixed at the label's perennial rate, is the strongest common option. For keeping ground bare for months, a residual vegetation killer like Ortho GroundClear Year Long is stronger, but it can harm tree roots. Mixing any product above its label rate does not make it stronger and often makes it work worse.

faqs.q: What weed killer works without killing grass?
faqs.a: A selective lawn herbicide kills weeds without killing grass. Tenacity spares most cool-season lawn grasses while killing many broadleaf weeds and crabgrass, and three-way broadleaf products handle dandelions and clover. Check the label's grass list first, because some products injure bermudagrass, St. Augustine or centipede. Never use a non-selective product on a lawn you want to keep.

faqs.q: What is the best rain proof weed killer?
faqs.a: No weed killer is rainproof the moment it lands, but many systemic concentrates, including Roundup Super Concentrate, become rainfast within a short time once the spray dries on the leaves. The label lists the exact rainfast period. Spray on a dry morning with no rain forecast for the rest of the day, and keep spray off pavement where rain carries it away.

faqs.q: How long does weed killer take to work?
faqs.a: Contact sprays and 20% vinegar wilt young weeds within hours in warm sun. Systemic products such as glyphosate show yellowing in several days and a full kill in one to two weeks. Selective lawn herbicides often take two to three weeks and sometimes a second application. Cool or dry weather slows all of them, so spray actively growing weeds.

faqs.q: Is weed killer safe for pets once it dries?
faqs.a: For most liquid herbicides, the label says people and pets can return once the spray has dried, which often takes a few hours on a warm, dry day. Granular products frequently need watering in first. Follow your specific label, keep pets inside during and after spraying, and store containers securely, since chewed bottles and spilled concentrate cause most pet poisonings.

faqs.q: Does vinegar work as a weed killer?
faqs.a: Yes, on young annual weeds. Horticultural vinegar at 20% acetic acid burns down leaves within hours in warm sun, but it does not move into roots, so established perennials like dandelions usually regrow. At that strength the label warns of serious eye damage, so wear goggles and gloves. Household 5% vinegar is much weaker and only affects tiny seedlings.

bottomLine: Buy the chemistry that fits the job, not the strongest jug. A selective product such as Tenacity handles weeds in a lawn, a systemic concentrate like Roundup or Compare-N-Save clears beds and fence lines to the roots, a residual killer like Ortho GroundClear belongs only on ground that should stay bare with no tree roots below, and Preen keeps a clean bed clean. Then follow the label for rate, timing, rainfast window and pet re-entry, spray only the weed on a calm, dry morning, and one bottle will go further and work better.
